nodes.question: Who is responsible for identifying and releasing the captured specimens in live trapping studies?
nodes.answer: Small mammal experts are responsible for identifying and releasing the captured specimens on site.
nodes.paragraph: So, for every study with live trap- ping paperwork is required to obtain exceptions of the men- tioned laws for the specific study sites. Exceptions granted might call for frequent checking intervals for live traps in the field. Captured specimens need to be identified and released on site by small mammal experts. Thus, legal requirements, manpower and scientific training of field workers are impor - tant when considering large scale and long-term routine sur - veys using live-traps. Consequently, the use of non-invasive methods is becom- ing increasingly important for documenting small mammal distribution, and will be the main, if not the only, accepted method to do so in the near future. Some non-invasive meth- ods such as owl pellet analysis have already been in use for some time, while others have been developed specifi- cally for one or a few species. All have both advantages and limitations. Mammal Research Owl pellet analysis is a well-established method to obtain small mammal remains, but has limitations for large scale monitoring, as a) the application is limited to areas where relevant birds of prey co-occur (for small mammals mainly the barn owl Tyto alba and tawny owl Strix aluco); b) the prey preferences of the birds of prey present a bias; c) a limited range of preferred hunting grounds; and d) only the locality where the pellet is regurgitated is known, but not the locality and habitat where the prey was captured (e.g.
